patient.chief_complaint: Stepwise decline in memory and organisation over three years since a stroke, with a further step after a visual episode
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Chiara Venturi is a 73-year-old retired French teacher who attends with her husband. Three years ago she was admitted elsewhere with left arm weakness and inattention to the left side; she was told she had had a stroke, was discharged on aspirin, and no cardiac monitoring beyond an inpatient ECG was performed. Her husband dates the first change to the months after that admission: she stopped preparing lessons for the private pupils she still taught, and began to need lists for tasks she had always held in her head. Fourteen months ago she had twenty minutes of blurred vision in the right field, which was attributed to migraine although she has never had migraine. In the weeks after it she gave up the private teaching altogether and twice mislaid the household bills. Between the two events she was stable, and her husband is emphatic that the changes were sudden rather than gradual. Her memory improves with prompting about context; her difficulty is with planning and with holding several things in mind. She has no headache, no seizures, no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment. Her pulse is regular today at 76, though frequent extra beats are palpable, and she has never been told she has an irregular heartbeat.

mri.impression: Multi-infarct pattern with chronic infarcts in the right middle cerebral and left posterior cerebral artery territories plus a left thalamic lacune, on a background of only Fazekas 1 white matter change. The bihemispheric multi-territory distribution indicates a cardioembolic source; the absence of microbleeds supports the safety of anticoagulation once a source is documented.

findings: Sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial complexes, including two couplets

Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria
ecg.interpretation: Sinus rhythm with frequent atrial ectopy and left ventricular hypertrophy. Frequent premature atrial complexes are a recognised marker of atrial cardiopathy and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; a single ECG in sinus rhythm does not exclude it, and in a patient with infarcts in two arterial territories the search must continue.

labs.interpretation: LDL 116 mg/dL is above target for a patient with established cerebrovascular disease. Reversible causes are excluded: TSH, B12 and folate normal, RPR non-reactive, HIV negative. Renal function is normal, which is relevant to anticoagulant dosing if a source is found.

cardiac_monitoring.impression: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with a 4.9% burden, previously undocumented. This is the embolic source for the multi-territory infarct pattern and it converts management from antiplatelet to anticoagulant therapy.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.query: vascular cognitive impairment diagnostic criteria and secondary prevention

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type, cardioembolic, secondary to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation identified on prolonged monitoring

differential.key_features: Stepwise course with dateable events, cue-responsive recall, preserved medial temporal lobes, and three infarcts that account for the deficits
Fazekas 1 burden is far below the threshold for attributing a dementia to small-vessel disease
No haemodynamically significant carotid disease, and no single artery can supply two territories in opposite hemispheres
The visual episode was misattributed to migraine in a patient with no migraine history; the left occipital infarct on MRI is the explanation
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Two dateable steps — a left hemispheric stroke and a right visual field event — with a stable plateau between them, cue-responsive memory, and executive-predominant loss of instrumental function

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 21/30 with executive and attentional predominance, cue-responsive recall, and residual constructional difficulty from the right hemispheric lesion

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; LDL above target and renal function documented ahead of a possible anticoagulation decision

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Chronic infarcts in two arterial territories in opposite hemispheres plus a thalamic lacune, Fazekas 1 white matter change, and no microbleeds — an embolic pattern with no contraindication to anticoagulation

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation as the embolic source and for the left ventricular hypertrophy of chronic hypertension
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial complexes and left ventricular hypertrophy — no fibrillation captured, so the embolic source remains unexplained and prolonged monitoring is required

optimal_actions.action: Image the extracranial carotid arteries to establish whether a large-artery source accounts for the cortical infarcts
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral minor plaque without flow limitation, which cannot explain infarcts in two territories in opposite hemispheres

optimal_actions.action: Order prolonged ambulatory rhythm monitoring: a single ECG in sinus rhythm does not exclude paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and finding it converts management from risk-factor control to anticoagulation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation captured — 4 episodes over 26 days, the longest 3 hours 40 minutes — establishing the embolic source and the indication for anticoagulation

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patchy multi-domain deficits with preserved recognition, fitting discrete lesions rather than a degenerative gradient

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Start anticoagulation for the documented paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and stop the aspirin, raise the statin to reach an LDL below 70 mg/dL, tighten blood-pressure control toward a systolic below 130 mmHg, and arrange a formal driving assessment given the residual visuospatial deficit
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticoagulation started on the strength of documented paroxysmal fibrillation with the antiplatelet stopped, vascular targets set, and driving formally assessed rather than left to self-restriction

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Establish the stepwise course and date each step against a clinical event
Obtain an ECG and, when it shows sinus rhythm in a patient with multi-territory infarcts, proceed to prolonged monitoring rather than stopping
Obtain brain MRI, count the infarcts by territory, and check SWI for microbleeds before anticoagulating
Image the carotid arteries to exclude a large-artery mechanism
Anticoagulate once paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is documented and stop the antiplatelet
Reattribute the visual episode previously called migraine to the occipital infarct, since it changes the mechanism assessment
Assess driving formally given the residual visuoconstructional deficit
contraindicated_actions: Do not accept a single sinus-rhythm ECG as excluding atrial fibrillation in a patient with infarcts in more than one territory
Do not continue aspirin together with a new anticoagulant without a separate coronary indication
Do not treat this as small-vessel disease on the strength of Fazekas 1 change
Do not leave a driving decision to the patient's own restriction when a visuospatial deficit is documented
key_reasoning_points: One ECG in sinus rhythm excludes nothing: paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is by definition intermittent, and in an unexplained multi-territory infarct pattern the yield of prolonged monitoring justifies it
Frequent premature atrial complexes are a marker of atrial cardiopathy and raise the pre-test probability of paroxysmal fibrillation
The lesion distribution — two territories, opposite hemispheres — is what makes the search for a proximal source obligatory
Checking SWI for microbleeds is part of the anticoagulation decision, not an academic exercise
A visual episode labelled migraine in a patient who has never had migraine deserves re-examination; here the occipital infarct explains it and adds a second territory to the count

red_herrings.data_point: A single ECG in sinus rhythm
red_herrings.intended_effect: Concludes that there is no atrial fibrillation and that the mechanism must be small-vessel or large-artery disease
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A sinus-rhythm ECG with frequent atrial ectopy in a patient with multi-territory infarcts mandates prolonged monitoring; the 30-day recorder captured a 4.9% fibrillation burden

red_herrings.data_point: A previous diagnosis of migraine with aura
red_herrings.intended_effect: Removes the visual episode from the vascular count and keeps the infarct burden apparently confined to one hemisphere
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: She has no migraine history, and the left occipital infarct on MRI accounts for the episode, adding a second arterial territory

key_educational_points: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is missed by single ECGs; prolonged monitoring is required when the infarct pattern is embolic and unexplained
Frequent premature atrial complexes raise the probability of occult fibrillation
Microbleed assessment on SWI belongs to the anticoagulation decision
A first episode labelled migraine deserves review when no migraine history exists
